title: Bad Company
full_review:
Coming on the heels of “The Sum of All Fears” which also dealt with nuclear terrorism, the comedy-drama “Bad Company” (Touchstone) may suffer from bad timing. Although it is popcorn entertainment with some thrilling action sequences, the uneven film hits a little too close to home for comfort with its plot about fanatical terrorists gaining possession of a suitcase-sized nuclear weapon. And even despite its star billing of Anthony Hopkins and Chris Rock, “Bad Company” may not be able to transcend audience feeling about not wanting to be exposed to a story about nuclear weapons in the wrong hands in their entertainment choices when there is enough real news about such horrific possibilities.

Hopkins portrays steely CIA agent Oakes, a man who genuinely believes in “duty to country.” Somber opening scene places Oakes in Prague with his Harvard-educated, highly trained partner Kevin Pope (Rock) haggling with a Russian black-marketer Vas (Peter Stormare) over the price of a compact nuclear weapon. The rapid-fire action that follows has a rival bidder make his presence known, fatally wounding Pope as he saves Oakes life.

The film then cuts to the laughs that Rock fans maybe expecting. Rock reappears as Jake Hayes, a fast-talking, streetwise hustler separating folks from their cash by winning chess games and scalping tickets. Jake has no idea that he had a twin brother separated from him at birth. Oakes and his team appear and persuade Jake to pose as his brother for the good of the country and a boat load of money.

Director Joel Schumacher procures some funny moments out of the nine training days the CIA operatives have to prepare Jake before returning to Prague to seal the deal. But what is missing in these scenes, and throughout the rest of the film, is any connection between Rock and Hopkins. As if to counter Rock’s high-spirited acting, Hopkins offers a very restrained performance. But the result is a rather bland, remote character who clearly has a conscience but little else to make him a compelling character. As Pope, the secret agent, Rock mistakes stiffness for formality. Yet even in his cardboard portrayal of the agent, it seems like he might break out at any moment into his characteristic wide-eyed, toothy grin.� Playing Jake, a role more in keeping with his comedic talents, Rock fares better. Surprisingly, he is better when Jake stands up for himself, angrily telling off Oakes’ snide, condescending boss in a memorable scene, than when he plays the wise-cracking fool shouting out silly quips as he avoids being shot or stabbed.

The action sequences can be exciting, particularly a car chase through the countryside outside of Prague, but they can also be quite intense. When one of the rival bidder’s henchmen unsuccessfully tries to kill Jake (thinking he is still Pope) and is cornered, his chooses to leap off a tall building, reinforcing the now all-too-familiar persona of the suicide terrorist. And Schumacher doesn’t just show you his hurtle downward, but in quick flashes, his landing and a closeup of his face, which is probably more than most viewers want to see.

Skimpy characterization detracts from the film as well. Oakes’ team is strictly one-dimensional, although the actors try hard to make their presence felt. The identity of the rival bidder (Matthew Marsh) is revealed to be a ruthless terrorist from Yugoslavia intent on blaming the United States for the status of things around the world. But he’s just an ugly mug without much more to his character other than a taste for American bloodshed. The film’s protracted ending wears the viewer down, with it’smany twists and turns, and especially because it is these scenes that vividly show the real potential for nuclear terrorism.

“Bad Company” was initially to be in theaters last fall but the release was postponed to give it some distance from the Sept. 11 attack. A scene toward the end of film offers a nod to patriotism, but seems to have been inserted at the last moment for effect. However, neither time nor this scene might be able to warm the chill some viewers may feel as a result of the slick story’s close resemblance to real world events.

Due to intermittent violence with a few intense action sequences, brief sexual suggestiveness and sporadic crass words with an instance of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
